# Assignment 4

## What are the practical approaches for reducing the expected new data error, according to the book?

The book mentions several approaches to reducing the expected new data error.
If possible, one should try to increase the amount of training data, as this
typically leads to a smaller expected new data error and a smaller
generalisation gap (the gap between the average training data error
and the average expected new data error). Furthermore, the book mentions the
relationship between the expected training error and the model complexity. A
high model complexity usually decreases the training error, but also
the generalisation gap. Conversely, a lower model complexity leads to a higher
training error, but also a lower generalisation gap. A good middle
ground to aim for is therefore a scenario where neither the generalisation
gap nor the expected training error is zero. By evaluating the expected new
data error and the training error via cross-validation, one can conclude that
if the calculated expected new data error and the training error are similar,
the model is possibly underfit and might benefit from an increased model
complexity. Furthermore, if the training error is zero and the calculated
expected new data error is not, the model is possibly overfit and might
benefit from decreasing the complexity. [p. 76-77]

## What important aspect should be considered when selecting minibatches, according to the book?

It is very important to make sure that all different mini-batches are
balanced and representative of the whole data set. If we have a big data
set with a lot of different possible output classes and use mini-batches
that are not balanced some of the mini-batches might not contain all of
the output classes and are therefor not a good representation of the
full data set. This will give bad approximations of the gradient for the
full data set. [p. 125]


## Provide an example of modifications in a loss function and in data that can be done to take into account the data imbalance, according to the book

To account for imbalance, a loss function can be modified using class weighting.
This modification signs a higher penalty weight to misclassifications of the
minority class compared to the majority class. In the book they give the example
of the loss for the minority class being multiplied by a factor C to make the
model prioritize its correct prediction. Similarly for the modification of data,
the book suggests duplicating the data points in the minority class by a 
factor C. This duplication makes the model see the minority class C times more,
giving it more importance in training. [p. 101-102]
